entry.title: Board games already solved agent coordination
entry.content:
After Plan, then let go I kept going down the list. WEGO is one turn structure among many, and most of the others have a counterpart in how we build agents. Most of the best ones come from the German-style board games that have always fascinated me, the Autorenspiele: games by a named author, whose name the Spiele-Autoren-Zunft wants “zumindest auf der Coverseite der Verpackung sowie in der Spielanleitung”, at least on the front of the box and in the rules.

A Eurogame is, at its core, a carefully tuned answer to one question: who may act, when, and at what cost. That is also the question an agent harness has to answer.

Turn structureA game that uses itThe agent counterpart
I go, you goChessthe ReAct loop: act, observe, act again
Everyone plans, then all resolvesDiplomacyplan-then-execute
Programmed actionsRoboRallya plan written as a queue of tool calls, where a small early mistake compounds
Role selectionPuerto Ricoan orchestrator that picks a task every worker then carries out
Worker placementCaylusparallel agents contending for shared resources: locks, rate limits, a single deploy slot
AuctionsModern Artmarket-based task allocation, the contract net
Deck-buildingDominioncurating the tool set and the context
Cooperation with limited talkHanabiagents that must infer what another agent knows
Automathe solo modes of the Automa Factorysimulated users for evaluation

Some of these are more than analogies. In Puerto Rico each player picks one role per round, every player then performs that role’s action, and the one who picked it gets a small privilege. That is a supervisor handing the same instruction to many workers, with the supervisor’s own share decided by the choice. Reid G. Smith’s contract net protocol (1980) allocates tasks among autonomous nodes by announcement and bidding, which is an auction table with the art removed. And Hanabi is not only like an agent benchmark, it is one: The Hanabi Challenge (Bard and others, 2019) proposes it as a research domain because it “elevates reasoning about the beliefs and intentions of other agents to the foreground.”

The Automa is my favourite. An automa is a small deck of cards that plays the opponent in a solo game: draw a card, follow its icons. Morten Monrad Pedersen founded the Automa Factory to build them for other publishers. Punchboard’s review of solo modes lists the games that “will never work for solo”: “Social deduction, auction games, take-that mechanics, party games.” They are the games where the other player’s mind is the game. Replace “opponent” with “user” and that is the honest limit of every simulated user in an agent eval: a deck of cards can stand in for behaviour, not for intent.

The general lessons come from what Eurogames value:

  • Few actions, each one costly. A Euro gives you two or three meaningful moves a round, not twenty. An agent with a small, typed action surface does better than one with fifty loose tools, which is also what Piet and others argue for web agents: typed site interfaces instead of clicks.
  • Indirect interaction. You rarely attack anyone in a Euro; you take the space they needed. Agents that coordinate through shared state are easier to reason about than agents that message each other.
  • Open information, little luck. The outcome follows from the decisions, so you can replay a game and see why you lost. That is what you want from a trace.
  • A known end. Every Euro has a visible end trigger, and good players plan backwards from it. Agents are bad at knowing when to stop; a budget or an end condition does that job.
  • Playtesting. A Euro is played hundreds of times before its numbers are fixed. Evals are the same work.

For Waterfront the table reads the other way round. The weekly order sheet already sits between WEGO and worker placement: lieutenants are workers, the city’s docks and warehouses are action spaces, and two gangs choosing the same pier on the same night is exactly the kind of coincidence the week should produce. Board games got there first, agent builders arrived later, and I am happy to borrow from both.

References

  • Spiele-Autoren-Zunft, 11-Punkte-Liste, on naming the author on the box.
  • Reid G. Smith, The Contract Net Protocol: High-Level Communication and Control in a Distributed Problem Solver, IEEE Transactions on Computers, C-29(12), 1980.
  • Nolan Bard and others, The Hanabi Challenge: A New Frontier for AI Research, arXiv:1902.00506, 2019; Artificial Intelligence 280, 2020.
  • Julien Piet and others, Web Agents Should Adopt the Plan-Then-Execute Paradigm, arXiv:2605.14290, 2026.
  • Shunyu Yao and others, ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models, arXiv:2210.03629, 2022.
  • Punchboard, Solo Modes in Board Games, Part Two: Automa.
  • Puerto Rico and Caylus, Wikipedia.

entry.title: Plan, then let go
entry.content:
While working on the design of Waterfront, the game I am sketching as a successor to Gangsters: Organized Crime, I went looking for the name of the rhythm I loved in it: give your orders with the clock stopped, then watch the week play out and do not touch it. Wargamers call it WEGO, “we go”, as opposed to the alternating “I go, you go” of classic turns. Everyone plans in secret, everything resolves at once. Diplomacy works this way on paper, Combat Mission and Frozen Synapse on screen.

The same shape turned up, under a different name, in the work I do during the day. In agent architectures it is called plan-then-execute, and it is the counterpart to the ReAct loop, where the model reasons, calls a tool, reads the result, and decides the next step, over and over. A plan-then-execute agent drafts the whole sequence of tool calls first, and then ordinary code or smaller models run it without asking the planner again.

The three phases are the same in both worlds:

PhaseIn the gameIn the agent
Planthe weekly order sheet: who goes where, with whom, and what to do if it goes wrongthe planner writes the full graph of tool calls, with branches
Lock inthe week starts; no orders change until it endscontrol passes to the executor; the plan is fixed
Executethe city runs, schedules cross, you watchthe steps run; the planner sees the outcome at the end

The reason for the lock is different in each. In the game, the lock is where the fun comes from: you cannot rescue a bad plan mid-week, so planning carries the weight, and the week becomes a story you did not write. In the agent, the lock is a security property. Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections (Beurer-Kellner and others, 2025) puts it plainly: “A prompt injection cannot force the LLM into executing a tool that is not part of the defined plan.” Untrusted text read during execution can still bend the arguments of a planned call, the paper notes, but it cannot add a new one. This year a Berkeley group went further and argued in Web Agents Should Adopt the Plan-Then-Execute Paradigm (Piet and others, 2026) that web agents should fix their program before reading any live page, since pages mix in text from sellers, reviewers and advertisers.

The trade-off is also the same. Plan-then-execute suits work where the big picture matters more than the next step and where reacting to what you see is risky or expensive. It suits poorly work where you cannot know the next step until you see the result of this one. A player in Waterfront who wants to react to every event would be playing the wrong game, and an agent exploring an unknown codebase is better off in a loop.

What I like is that the friction is the point in both. The player and the planner give up control at the moment it would be most tempting to keep it, and in exchange they get something that cannot happen while they hold on: a week that surprises you, an agent whose control flow nobody else can rewrite. I spend my days on the second and my evenings on the first, and it is a small pleasure to find they are one idea.

References

  • Luca Beurer-Kellner and others, Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections, arXiv:2506.08837, 2025.
  • Julien Piet and others, Web Agents Should Adopt the Plan-Then-Execute Paradigm, arXiv:2605.14290, 2026.
  • Shunyu Yao and others, ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models, arXiv:2210.03629, 2022.
  • Combat Mission, Wikipedia.

entry.title: Future Cop: L.A.P.D., a duel between genres
entry.content:
One of the most fun things I played on the PlayStation was a side mode in a game about police robots. Future Cop: L.A.P.D. came out in 1998, set in a Los Angeles of 2098, and next to its campaign it had a mode called Precinct Assault. Two players, one arena, one base each. You pilot the X1-Alpha, a machine that switches between a fast hover car and a slow, heavily armed walking mech. You drive out to capture turrets and outposts, you spend what they earn on hovertanks that roll toward the other base on their own, and you buy helicopters to shoot down the tanks coming at yours. The first tank to break into a base ends the match.

What made it work was that you were two things at once. You were the soldier, in the middle of the fighting, escorting your tanks through the turrets and hunting the other player. And you were the general, deciding whether the next credits went into attack or defence. Every minute you spent driving back to defend was a minute your own push went without you.

It was not the first game to try this. Herzog Zwei did something close on the Mega Drive in 1989, with a transforming mech of its own, and the Wikipedia article on Future Cop notes that the difference is that you can help your army reach the other base yourself. Precinct Assault is sometimes counted as an early form of the MOBA, and the genre that followed kept the lanes and the units that walk them. But it dropped the economy and the general, and it went from one against one to five against five. I have not found a game since that does exactly what Precinct Assault did.

The version I would like to build is a one-against-one DotA in a setting closer to Terminator: a ruined city, machines on both sides, one transforming unit per player that is both your hero and your commander. Capture a factory and it produces infantry. Capture a ridge and it holds a turret. Everything you own is something the other player can take, and the only way to protect it is to be somewhere, which means not being somewhere else.

References

  • Future Cop: L.A.P.D., Wikipedia.
  • Herzog Zwei, Wikipedia.

entry.title: Gangsters: Organized Crime, orders for the week
entry.content:
The other game I keep coming back to from 1998 is Gangsters: Organized Crime, by Hothouse Creations for Eidos. It is set in New Temperance, a fictional suburb of Chicago during Prohibition, and you start as a small-time crime boss with a handful of hoods and a lot of ambition.

What made it unlike anything else was the rhythm. Each turn you sat down and planned: which lieutenant takes which crew, which shops get visited for protection money, which business opens next. Then you let go, and the working week played out in real time on the city map while you watched your orders meet everyone else’s. Some of it went as planned. Much of it did not, and the next planning session started from whatever the week had left you.

Underneath was a whole small society. Hoods were people with skills, fists and knives and intelligence, recruited from gyms, pool halls and the unemployment office. Money came from protection rackets and from businesses, some legal and some not, and you needed an accountant to launder it and a lawyer to get your people out when they were arrested. Run things carelessly and the police and the FBI started paying attention. And there were three ways to win: take out every rival gang, get yourself elected mayor, or go straight and build a legitimate empire without the law on your back.

That last one is the part I think about most. The same machinery, the hoods, the money, the city, served three different stories, and only one of them was about violence. Most strategy games give you a world to conquer. Gangsters gave you a world to run, with the option of becoming respectable in it.

I have not played anything like it since, and like Precinct Assault, it sits in my head as a design worth picking up again: plan in turns, live with the consequences in real time, and let the player decide what winning means.

References

  • Gangsters: Organized Crime, Wikipedia.
